utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Indah Susanti for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and we have two interns with us, Ms. Louise Beck and Mr. Paul Derohannesian, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Theodora Oprea and Eelke Daatselaar appearing for Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness resumes the stand, there is a statement which the Chamber has to make. First of all, I was required yesterday afternoon to give a certain answer in respect of the ancillary services which support the work of the Chamber and based on the information at hand up to the time that we would have risen yesterday in terms of what counsel would have represented, I confirmed that we will not be sitting next week. In addition to that, the -- for reasons which the parties and counsel are all aware and which I needn't go into details about because some of it was taken in private session, it appears to us that when the present witness is released, upon the rising of the Court, we will take the adjournment to Monday the 11th of July at which time we expect Mr. Krgovic to open, and bring his -- he -- my recollection is he indicated his opening statement would take no more than one session, so we expect that his first witness would be available on the 11th of July. Thank you. So could the usher please escort the witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say, while the witness is coming, there are probably certain technical matters that need to be attended to in respect of starting the second accused's case before the first one is finished, but we can deal with that when the witness is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HAL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I had to remind myself as to where we are. Before Ms. Korner resumes her cross-examination, I remind you, I give you the usual warning, that you are still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to return very briefly to two matters that we dealt with yesterday. First of all, the question of whether Mr. Blagojevic, Sasa Blagojevic, was actually working for you during May, and you told the Court yesterday you thought he was in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please, 20214, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is described as a bulletin of daily events, it's actually sent up to the ministry of interior in Sarajevo and not to the CSB Sarajevo, dated the 27th of May, 1992. There's a typed name, Sasa Blagojevic, and some kind of initialing. I don't know, are you able to say whether those -- that's the way he'd sign?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, I don't want to interrupt, but Ms. Korner just said that it's actually sent up to the Ministry of Interior in Sarajevo; based on what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's from the -- you're quite right. Sorry. It's headed the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but all the documents despite where they are coming from are headed Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know where this is coming from. It's headed the "Ministry of the Interior." It's headed "Bulletin of Daily Events," dated the 27th of May. Can you tell me whether you recognise the initials as those of Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recognise these initials. This is a bulletin of the Ministry of the Interior. If it was the bulletin of the Security Services Centre, then it would have clearly said "Security Services Centre, Romanija-Birac." That's our masthead that you can see in all our documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm only interested in does it appear -- was there any other Sasa Blagojevic that you know of who was working at the ministry in Vrace on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that there is another Sasa Blagojevic. I'm not sure whether he worked in the police at the time. He works in the police now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do the events that are dealt with in this bulletin are all the names of the places within the greater Sarajevo area, if I can put it that way, Bosanska Surbata Street and Petrovacka Street?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, all I want to know is whether Mr. Blagojevic was in fact working on the 27th of May, whether this makes you change your mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the very end of May. I don't know whether he worked at the time or not. As far as I know in April and May he was in Gorazde, so since this is the very end of May, he may have returned by then. I said April and May. He definitely spent some time here, enough that he went to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please -- I want to return, please, to the question of the JNA's occupation with the airport which is linked with the establishment of Novo Sarajevo station SJB. Could we have up on the screen, please, the document which is 20213.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is apparently the statement of Mr. Kenan Delic, inspector in the MUP, and do you remember I asked you yesterday whether you knew a Kenan Delic who worked at the airport and you said you did. This apparently is a report on the JNA take-over of the airport. It's got a signature. Do you -- would you recognise Mr. Delic's signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, it's headed "Report on the JNA Take-over of the Sarajevo Airport." He says he worked, if you look at the first paragraph, first sentence, 4th of April this year to the afternoon of the 5th of April. He was at the Sarajevo Airport Police Station. And then there's a description about the, effectively, what was already the split in the MUP. Second paragraph, does that begin: "In the afternoon of the 5th of April, having selected the staff, I left a reinforced shift at the airport and sent a portion of the manpower to rest for a couple of hours"? If we go to the sentence towards the end of the second paragraph: "From time to time I had telephone contacts with the shift commander, Mr. Zahid Hodzic," and then, "who informed me that it was quiet at the airport. However, in the evening he informed me that he had heard from the flight control officer" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "that a JNA unit was en route to the airport from Rajlovac. The unit had six tanks and a couple of personnel carriers," and he goes on, and I don't want to go any further because the actual detail is irrelevant. Would you be prepared to accept now, Mr. Tusevljak, that the JNA went into the airport on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do object because I think if Ms. Korner is putting to the witness the statement of another person it should be read until the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to spend any time on it. What I will do is give Mr. Tusevljak a hard copy of it which he can read, it's very short, over the break, and I'll deal with it as the last, hopefully the last, thing I'm going to ask him, if that's satisfactory to Mr. Zecevic. May I say, I'm not seeking to exhibit it; it's purely to see whether he's prepared to change his answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to move, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Didn't the witness change his answers already in making the difference between Serb take-over and JNA take over, and he admitted to the JNA take-over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't -- it was the date I don't think he was agreeing to, Your Honours. That's all. I'm only concerned about the date. Everything else is agreed, it's just the date. And the reason is, as Your Honours knows, because it's linked to the Novo Sarajevo incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I would now like, please, to deal with, yes, one other matter relating to disciplinary. As far as the reserve police are concerned, could we have up again, please, the document you were shown, 1D190, which is tab 76 of the Defence bundle, Mr. Tusevljak, so you've got the actual hard-copy document there. This was the report from Vlasenica on the 6th of August in response to a request to know about disciplinary proceedings, I think, and the removal of police officers who committed offences. "Based on documented criminal offences, the Vlasenica Public Security Station filed 14 criminal reports against 14 perpetrators of which 13 were for aggravated theft and one for murder. All the individuals involved are members of the reserve police force. And the equipment they had been issued with was taken away with [sic] them immediately by the Vlasenica Public Security Station. Because of breaches of work discipline, 35 members of the reserve force were made to return the equipment they had been issued with and were removed from work." So is this the situation, as regards reserve police, there were two sanctions. First, that they could be made to surrender all the equipment and were removed from work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were reserve policemen. As far as I know, they could have been removed only because they did not actually work in the MUP of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Right, that they were called up to serve for certain periods. But the way of disciplining them was to make sure that they were no longer reserve policemen and that they no longer had equipment; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think there were no disciplinary proceedings. I think that they only returned their equipment. And if there was a report, they would have been tried. If there was no report, they would probably be transferred to the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Just pause for a moment. If a person who was a reserve police officer committed a disciplinary infraction which did not amount, however, to the possibility of a criminal act, then the remedy was to remove from him all the equipment, his ID card, and the like; is that right? If you don't know the answer because you've never dealt with disciplinary proceedings, Mr. Tusevljak, then please say so.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I had no reserve policemen under me, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's fair enough. But -- and we can see also, however, that here the Vlasenica SJB had actually filed criminal reports against 14 members of the reserve police force; is that right? Well, I think we can all read that so it's otiose.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were shown a document by the Defence which is at tab 91, Exhibit 1D589 MFI. Tab 91 in the Defence bundle. This is the Crisis Staff of Vogosca issuing an order on the 26th of May about the release from prison of 154 people, going on to say 20 persons are left in the prison and are being operatively processed. Now, before we go any further, we've discussed operatively processing before. Are you prepared to accept that this was an expression used by a number of police in different places to mean interviewing those who had been taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, operative work means that checks are being made about these persons. It's basically about checks being made. You can call it whatever you want. But the men who wrote this, I already told you, I didn't know Zdravko Luketa, I heard about this name the first time when I looked at this document, so this is some sort of order that he issued. So I really, really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the reason I'm putting that to you, because you say that's a meaningless expression in this context, and I'm suggesting to you that it's an expression that we find in many police documents relating to prisoners, non-Serbs, who had been taken to let me call them detention institutions and meant interviewing them to find out what nationality they were, what they'd been doing, how they'd come to be there, or words to that effect. Now, are you prepared to accept that or not? If you're not, say so straightaway.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sort of order -- well, this is the first order of this kind that see. I haven't seen anything else similar. Operative work is a standard terminology for the police. Operative work can mean a lot of things. It's a very, very wide term. The meaning is very wide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. That will do. Thank you very much. Now, from that you were led on by -- from this document you were led on to ask [sic] questions about a Mr. Vlaco or the two Mr. Vlacos. At page 2246 of the transcript -- sorry, 22246, you in fact were shown another document about the suggestion -- the report which had the suggestion of appointing Mr. Brane Vlaco. Now, you were asked about Brane Vlaco, and you said this: "Brane Vlaco was an ex-employee of the white collar crime of the Sarajevo CSB. He might have been in some kind of management position. He was there when the war broke out because he was originally from Vogosca. He signed up to work in this police station, so he was an inspector in our centre before the war. "Do you know him personally? "Yes, I know him personally. "Did he have some kind of specific feature, mustache, beard? And you said: "At the time he had a mustache I think. Today that's true, but I haven't seen him for a number of years," leaving aside the slight inconsistency there, but never mind. And then you were asked: "What happened to him after this, did he become the chief of the crime prevention service at Vogosca SJB? "A. I don't think he did. And if he did by any chance, he then held that position for a very short period of time because soon after he left the area. "Q. Do you know where he when and what he did? "A. I think that for a while he was an inspector at the crime police administration in Bijeljina, the RS MUP, and then after that he moved to some other positions that were not within the MUP. "Q. Do you know what he does today? "A. I think that he is a banker nowadays." And then, slightly later, at - it was the next day - page 22348, you were taken back to that document from the beginning of July from Vogosca and it was put to you that there was a proposal that "Brane Vlaco be appointed chief of the crime police. Do you remember that?" And then you were asked: "... do you remember what his real name was? His first name?" And you think: "Branislav, I think. Branislav Vlaco ... Brane is just a nickname. "Do you know a person with the same last name but a different first name, namely Branko Vlaco? "Yes, I met that person sometime during the course of the war in 1992. "What do you know about this gentleman, Branko Vlaco? "I think" that "he was a retired policeman and that at the beginning of the war he was a prison warden, or sometime during 1992, I don't know exactly." Now, let's just get clear when you met this man who was the prison warden. Is that the man -- did you meet him by going to Vogosca, to the prison there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I met him -- whether it was in Vogosca or elsewhere, I don't know, but I met him sometime in 1992. I did not meet him in the prison because I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you can't say anything other than you met him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I met him sometime in 1992. And then after that I had a chance to get to know him better because later on in 1993 or 1994 he was transferred to work in the police again. And then in the meetings, in 1994 or maybe even 1995, I had the opportunity to get to know him better. So it was in the police, because the centre was then transferred from Lukavica to Ilidza and it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, there's no dispute in this case that the Vlaco who was the warden of this prison in Vogosca did in October 1992 become the commander of the SJB Vogosca. So is that when you met him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I'm telling you, I don't know when, but it was 1992. I even thought that he was appointed to that post in 1993 or maybe even later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, we've seen evidence and heard evidence about this, Mr. Tusevljak, so don't concern yourself. But I want to try and see if I can, with you, sort out these two different Vlacos. Would you accept that both Brane and Branko are short forms for the full -- or nicknames for the name Branislav?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I come from it's usual for nicknames like that to be thought up. Brane could be Branislav, Bratislava, Branko, Branimir, all that, really. It's just a nickname. No more than that. The short form of a name, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's agreed. Not that it matters whether I agree or not. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, first of all, at document 20209, which is tab 59 in the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This appears to be headed "Biography," and we can see it's got a signature and it says Vlaco, Branislav. Says he was born in 1957 and then can we go -- sorry, I've lost my own copy of this English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I slightly -- can we zoom in slightly on paragraph 2, please, on the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He then says that he went and worked in -- no, he was in Slovenia for six months, worked on business plans, blah, blah, and then at about the fifth line: "I spent the period from the 10th of February, 1984, until December 1986 on this job, then I was transferred to the republican SUP, i.e., the CSB Sarajevo, in the business of discovering and preventing high industry" -- it must be crime, "with emphasis on bank deals. I had been on this post until the beginning of the war, when I left for Vogosca where I took the job for housing and municipal services in the Serbian municipality of Vogosca." And so on and so forth. Now, that's the first man you described, is it, the one who was in the CSB, it would appear?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he says that he left the CSB at the beginning of the war, went to Vogosca, and took a job for housing. You may or may not know that, but did he leave the CSB Sarajevo at the beginning of the war? Had he gone by the time you started work there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood. This Sarajevo CSB is the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo of the republican secretariat of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is the centre that kept on existing until the 4th of April, 1992, the one where he worked. And he's talking about leaving that security centre -- Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. Sorry, what I'm trying to get: He certainly wasn't working for the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we're not talking about the Romanija-Birac centre. He left the Security Services Centre of the republican SUP in Sarajevo on the 4th of April, 1992. That was the one he left, not the Romanija-Birac centre, because the Romanija-Birac centre was not around on the 4th of April, 1992. It wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. But then it says he goes off at the beginning of the war to go into housing. Now could you have a look, please, at 20206, which is tab 35A. This is a report following a visit to the Svrake settlement. The commission established there are a certain number of free family houses, and don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the second page in English and the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report of the 14th of October and it shows that the commission who was dealing with this consisted of Brane Vlaco and two other people. So that appears to be, does it not, the man, the Vlaco who was at the CSB, left, and, according to his biography, went into housing; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen these documents before. I can't talk about Branislav Vlaco or Brane. I wasn't in the area. I didn't know about this. I looked at his CV and I found out for the first time that he was a member of this commission for housing issues in -- and public utilities in Vogosca municipality. That's when his name came forward. And I was right when I said that I didn't remember him being appointed chief -- crime police chief at all. If he held that position, it would only have been for a very short time because I couldn't even remember at the time. I know for a fact, nevertheless, that he was a member of the crime police administration at one point in time when I was there too, and we worked together. But is it the same Brane Vlaco or a different person going by the same name, it's difficult to say, because you see all these documents referring to Brane Vlaco. No names, just inverted commas, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say, Mr. Tusevljak, this is not entirely your fault, but this just happens to be something that has to be dealt with and it appears you're the only witness, and you were led to talk about him, who can deal with it. So, I'm sorry, I'm going to have to ask you: But as a matter of common sense, the Vlaco who signed that CV, I suppose one would call it, is the one who was in the CSB, the one who goes off into housing, and who in October of 1992 is dealing with housing that is available in Svrake; would you agree as a matter of common sense that's right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand this question. The matter of common sense. We all, I hope, have a common sense, so therefore -- well, yes, it's a matter for discussion, I agree. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour knows why I have to deal with this, and there's nothing else I can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I suggest, Ms. Korner, that the -- although usually we don't ask a fact witness to draw inferences, see what his comment is and then leave the rest for argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Tusevljak, that even though you've never seen those documents before, the proper inference that can be drawn from this is that the man that you knew who had been in the CSB went off into the housing commission and in October of 1992 was dealing with that housing?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's assume it's about the same person or assume it is the same person. It's an assumption. If you look at the CV, this is the housing commission, and then a reasonable deduction would be it's him, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the other Vlaco, shall we, the one who was running the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at document 20193, which is at 6A bis of the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an interview with the man Branko Vlaco who was commander of the Vogosca Prison, was commander. He is currently the chief of police in Vogosca. So it's clearly the man who went from the prison to Vogosca Police Station. Interview took place in his office. And he then explained that he'd been "a member of the federal Yugoslav police in this district. I retired a few months before the war in order to open a restaurant, serving only wild game. And when the war began, I was made commandant of the prison here in Vogosca." So, again, I appreciate this is not a document you've seen before, but would you again agree, as a matter of logic and inference, that this man who's being interviewed who was the prison warden and is then in the police in Vogosca is different from the man that you knew who had been in the CSB and then in the housing?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what I see in front of me is in English, which unfortunately I don't speak. I can't answer based on the document. I can answer based on the question you asked. These are two different persons. Brane Vlaco was a lawyer or a prison director, as he passes him himself off, and then after a while he became police commander at the Vogosca Police Station. And that's as much as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on this topic, I hope, could we have a look at P-- two more documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, can we have this document MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we can have it -- I'll have the whole bunch exhibited, Your Honours, if that's possible. The problem was they haven't been disclosed so I wasn't going to go there, but I would like them all exhibited, if I can, not just one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think I'm going to be gracious today and not object.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honours, can I have, please, exhibits 20209, tab 59, it's the biography, exhibited; 20206, tab 35A; and this one which is 20193, tab 6A bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the generosity, to borrow Mr. Zecevic's choice of words, in terms of the application that Ms. Korner has made, the Chamber's reservation is as to the relevance of these document, whether we aren't just adding paper unnecessarily. Could counsel enlighten us, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that the witness should take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tusevljak, could you please remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've just been practicing saying that name more often than Your Honour has. Your Honour, can I explain. It's a minor point but, it's one on which the Defence have been insisting. As you know, a Branko Vlaco was supposed to be a witness, and the Defence have now withdrawn him for whatever reason. And otherwise, all these matters could have been dealt with with him. There is no dispute as I understand it, and I'll accept any correction, that there were two persons by the name of Branislav Vlaco in Vogosca in 1992 and that on the 21st of July of 1992 a Branislav Vlaco was appointed the warden of Planja's House, about which Your Honours had heard so much. There's also no dispute that that one, the who was the warden of Planja's House, known as the Vogosca Prison, was in fact appointed the SJB Vogosca Police commander in October, which is the document P1519, and there's been testimony about that. The dispute is this: Whether the Branislav Vlaco who became the warden was a member of the SJB Vogosca prior to the 21st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what, if I may add, what turns on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We say that the police - and it's -- the Defence have made a huge issue out of this one - were in fact closely connected with the running of these prisons, and, in particular, this one. Otherwise, Your Honours, nobody -- and can I say, straightaway, it's Mr. Zecevic who brought this all up by asking the witness these questions, and I say I'm entitled to deal with it and that's the only Defence witness I can deal with this on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's precisely that I did -- that I did deal with this matter with this witness and that is precisely because it is disputed what Ms. Korner just said. Your Honours, basically there are two names, two first names, in the region which are sort of similar. One is Branko, B-r-a-n-k-o, Branko. And that is the person, Branko Vlaco, is the warden of Vogosca Prison. That is one person. The other person is Branislav Vlaco, who was a member of the CSB, returned to Vogosca, and went to the bank. Apparently within that time he was in the housing department of Vogosca municipality. Now, the position of the Office of the Prosecutor was because a certain person, Brano Vlaco, appears on the lists for payment in Vogosca SJB prior to July, they -- their position is that this concerns the Branko Vlaco, the prison warden. The allegation is that this person was a member of SJB and then he was appointed the prison warden and then returned to the SJB. Well, what we say is that is not the case. The case is that the Branislav Vlaco, the person who escaped from CSB Sarajevo, have been the member of the SJB for a short period of time, as this witness confirmed, that he was in the crime police of the SJB Vogosca when it was established in July for a short period of time, and then left, and that this person has nothing to do with Branko Vlaco, the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so, if I may ask you, Mr. Zecevic, the way I understand this is that crucial point is whether Branko Vlaco, the prison warden, would be on the MUP payroll; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, because that is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor, that this person since being a member of the MUP prior to become a prison warden and after that so therefore the MUP had -- something to do with the Planja's House, Naka's Garages, and all the other detention centres which existed in Vogosca, and we say that's not true and that there is -- that the connection through Branko Vlaco is a non-existent one. That is the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just to make sure, you just said that the witness confirmed that he, and this is about Brane, the housing man, let's say, that he was in the crime police of Vogosca when it was established in June for a short period of time. I want to come back to "the witness confirmed." Wasn't the witness saying he didn't know, and if he had been it would have been for such a short time that he didn't realise something in that vein? Or am I confusing ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 14, line 7, witness's answer: "That's when his name came forward. And I was right when I said that I didn't remember him ... appointed chief -- crime police chief at all. If he held that position, it would only have been for a very short time because I couldn't even remember at the time. I know for a fact, nevertheless, that he was a member of the crime police administration at one point in time when I was there too, and we worked together." And this is concerning Branislav Vlaco. Your Honours, there is a document which is Exhibit 1D106. It's the report of the 12th of July. In that report the inspectors that went to Vogosca are proposing that Vlaco, Brane be appointed chief of the crime prevention department in Vogosca SJB. Now, when I -- in the direct examination the witness confirmed that it is -- that this Brane Vlaco is in fact Branislav Vlaco, the one who came from the CSB and now is working in the bank. So it has nothing to do with the prison warden. And now on the cross-examination he confirmed that he knows that this person -- he doesn't know if he was actually appointed, but he knows that he worked in the crime prevention department and that he co-operated with him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's why, as you can see - sorry - it's a live issue and I think that it's small but it's live and the Defence have spent a great deal of time on it and I think, therefore, that all the documents should be admitted. I've got two further documents I want to put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Except that the documents that we've seen so far do not clearly resolve the issue of who Mr. Branko Vlaco then was. Where does he come from and did he have anything to do with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the Vlaco who was the prison warden says he worked for the MUP before that. Then he left to become -- to run a restaurant and, we say, then went back, became the warden, because he appears on the roll -- he went back to the police, became the warden and then finally ended up back as the commander. Whereas the other Vlaco, having left the -- having been, obviously, some kind of a businessman, then went to the white collar unit of the CSB Sarajevo and from then, according to his own biography, and it's clearly him, went into housing. And that's what he's doing. So he has nothing more to do with the police after he leaves the old CSB Sarajevo. That is our argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I may be of assistance, Your Honours, the document which you have in front of you confirms; it says "interview with Branko Vlaco, commandant of the Vogosca Prison from approximately May 1992 until November 1992, currently chief of police," and so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but we know that. But we know it's not right because we've got the appointment of Vlaco to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the Mr. Vlaco that you had on your witness list but you removed from your list, is that the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would hardly be wasting all this -- not wasting time, but effectively having to go through these matters with this witness if the real Mr. Vlaco was going to turn up, but he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that would have taken much more time, I'm afraid, than this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The documents are -- the three documents are admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are two more, Your Honours, that I want to deal with with the witness. I --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 20209 shall be given Exhibit P2364. 65 ter 20206 shall be given Exhibit P2365. And 65 ter 20193 shall be given Exhibit P2366. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thanks. Your Honours, just to remind Your Honours, can we have up, please, Exhibit P1506 to see how this has all arisen. It's tab 4C of our binder. It's dated the 28th of May, 1992. It's the nominal role of the active and reserve police at Vogosca. Could we go to the third page in English and the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At number 63 in May is listed a Brano Vlaco, which is again -- this is all, is it not, Mr. Tusevljak, Brano, Brane, Branko, whatever, are all names, short forms of Branislav?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm saying it once again. This is the first time that I see this list. Please, I'm on this job in Bosnia and Herzegovina too. There is a project called CIPS; it's a database containing identificational data of all people who have personal IDs. Do you think that there are only two persons called Brane Vlaco or maybe three, maybe even four, with the same name and also living in Vogosca? Sometimes we type in one name and 300 persons come up with the same first and last name who live in Bosnia and Herzegovina and then within those 300 we have to look for the particular one we are interested in. So I could now say, yes, that's the one, but I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I know you don't know, Mr. Tusevljak. Stop, please, for a moment. The trouble is, and I assume that Mr. Zecevic explained to you why he was asking these questions about the Mr. Vlacos when he proofed you, did he, Mr. Tusevljak? Did Mr. Zecevic explain to you that there was an argument going on between the Prosecution and the Defence about who the Vlaco was who was the prison warden and at the same time was on the list of police for Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that there should be anything at issue here. The one who was appointed the warden, and I don't know exactly when, he was the warden and then he came to work in the police. I thought it was in 1993, but it turns out it was in 1992. And then Branko Vlaco the former inspector in the CSB is a completely different person. Now, which one is on this list, I don't know. There is no way for me to know this. This is the first time that I see this list and I cannot know anything about this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct. That wasn't my question, though. Did Mr. Zecevic before you gave evidence, when you spoke to him, explain to you that he was going to ask you questions about Vlaco that had been in the CSB before the war and Vlaco who was the prison warden and then became the commander? Did Mr. Zecevic speak to you about that? That's the question, to which the answer is either "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he explain to you that the reason he was going to ask you about this was because there was a dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence about the Vlaco who was a member of the police, reserve police, in Vogosca in May and who then became -- and the prison warden person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was merely asked whether I knew both of them and whether I knew who was the warden and who was Brano Vlaco who worked in the CSB, and that I know. And as for the rest, the list, this is the first time that I see this list. And I cannot tell you which one is Brano Vlaco under number 63. I cannot say it's this one or that one. I really cannot say that. If there were only two of them, it would be simpler, but who knows?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you to look, please, at one final document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which, please, is at tab 6B, 20199.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a handwritten record of effectively another intercept again. It's a conversation on the 30th of June and it's recorded as a Branko Vlaco phoning from the Damjan --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to object. This document is -- does not have the audio file at all. This is just a document which we don't know the authenticity, we don't know who created it, and therefore it's not reliable for -- I mean, Ms. Korner is entitled to ask the question, but she cannot use this document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I can hardly ask the question without using the document. Your Honours, we are back to the intercept question again. This one -- can we just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very simple. The point of the matter is that Ms. Korner cannot state that this is a transcript of conversation of one person to the other person. There is no audio file. We don't know who said this is person Slobodan Zecevic or some other person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is, as I said, we're back to the -- the witness may take his headphones off, I suppose, again. If I can't rely, on, Your Honours, the name, the names that are given here, then it's absolutely pointless -- I mean, I can, I suppose, to a certain extent part of the conversation will make it clear that it's to do with these events, but it's absolutely pointless trying to use this document. And, as I say, in fact, I don't think -- this is not, definitely not one of the documents that Your Honours admitted, as I say, but it's part that -- Your Honours may recall that some of the intercept material was, in fact, handwritten records of conversations as opposed to audio files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But having regard for the reasons that Mr. Zecevic has given, I'm at a loss to see what use you can make of this document at this stage, if at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, why can't I use it? It's a record of an intercept. The fact that I can't call -- the fact that I can't call the maker doesn't go to whether it's admissible or whether I can use it to ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the whole point is: How can Ms. Korner say this is a record of an intercept. How? I mean, based on what? This is a document, handwritten document. We don't know the author. We don't know the authenticity. And there's no audio file. It cannot be said this is a record of the intercept of a conversation of two persons or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If that's the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I see if I can ask some questions about it and let's see where we go with that, about the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, without specifically referring to the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. -- oh, put your headphones back on. Mr. Tusevljak, do you recognise a number, telephone number, I think, 467-60 -- 680.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember this number. I don't know. I'm not in a habit of remembering phone numbers. I don't know the number. Number 4, well, it could be Ilidza. I think that maybe Ilidza used to be number 4. I think that phone numbers at Ilidza used to begin with number 4 before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Was there a problem in June of -- towards the end of June of there being a crime spree, as it were, where property was being robbed and broken into or broken into and robbed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in all the reports that we filed at the time we mentioned this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know whether the Vlaco who later became the commander of the police station in October knew Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. They probably knew each other in 1992. Whether they knew each other before that, I don't know, and I don't know when they met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you aware, though, that Mr. Cvijetic sent people to Vogosca on the 3rd of July to look at the crime situation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we have the report written by the operatives who went to Vogosca and then were chased away. That's what you are talking about, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was Mr. Cvijetic sending people down to Vogosca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the centre. He could decide when somebody would be sent to a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in the light of what Your Honours rule, I don't think I can take it any further than that. I don't know that it adds much to it because although the content is, to a certain extent, supported, without the names of the people who are speaking, it's meaningless. So Your Honours are not going to resile from my request to have -- to be able to put the speakers to him? I'm not going to -- sorry, resile from the denial of my request based on Mr. Zecevic's objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Ms. Korner, to the extent that a formal answer is required, the Chamber's of the view that you can't use this document any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, finally, on Vogosca, please, can we look, please, at document 20204, tab 8A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Should you take the break now or is this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd rather, if I may, I want to complete Vogosca and then go on towards, effectively, my last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is this still on the Vlaco/Vlaco issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, this is in the connection of the police with the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I had one question -- I don't know whether -- has the witness been asked simply whether he knows of the prison -- that the prison -- whether he knows or not that the prison warden was a member of the MUP before becoming prison warden? Just simply and bluntly the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think -- Your Honour is quite right, I don't think he has.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, do you know whether the man who was the prison warden and who later definitely was part of the Vogosca SJB, as commander, do you know whether he was in the police before he was a warden?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the police at Vogosca, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, as a reserve police officer in Vogosca. Do you know whether he was or wasn't?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we look, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have we got up 8A? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is one of a series of documents. Were you aware that authorised officials of the Vogosca SJB on the 7th of July, 1992, brought in two people to Mr. Vlaco, as the prison warden, two Muslims, it would appear?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time that I see this bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Were you aware in general terms from being chief of the crime police at the CSB that in Vogosca members of the SJB were bringing in non-Serbs to the custody of Mr. Vlaco's prison?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I knew that there was some sort of a prison there. Here we see that these persons were suspected of hiding members of the TO. So I don't know exactly within whose jurisdiction that was, but I have to say that I knew nothing about this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at 955D1, which is a 65 ter number, and it's at tab 16A of the bundle -- of our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Around about the same time, 27th of July, a Mr. Nijaz Suko was taken from Vogosca by the state security, a member of state security. Mr. Rifet Durak also taken from the Vogosca by an authorised official of the Ilijas SJB. And Mr. Rasim Muharemovic was taken from the Vogosca prison on the same day by the prison warden for the purposes of exchange. Now, first of all, were you aware that not only Vogosca was bringing them there, but other SJBs and indeed state security appear to have been taking people out of this prison?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see anything like that here. I'm not sure whether they were bringing people in. Is some people were brought in, then they must have been people from whom it would have been established that they were members of enemy formations. However, here I see that this is the person belonging to the state security, and I have to tell you that I never received any sort of information from the state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but were you being given information that apparently prisoners, first of all, were being taken from the prison by other SJBs, in this case Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we in the centre were never informed about these activities. You can see that clearly from our documents. Nobody informed us about these activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that prisoners were being used -- non-Serbs were being used to -- as parts of exchanges with the other side?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were exchanges all the time. Serbs were exchanged for Bosniaks and the other way around, but this was done by some municipal committees, Crisis Staffs, and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Weren't, in fact, people like this Rasim Muharemovic actually being carted off to prison in order to be used for exchanges; isn't that what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we can see from this bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, I don't think you quite understood what I was putting to you. I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Tusevljak, that these were civilians who had done nothing, who were being taken off to prison purely and simply so that they could be used as exchanges, for exchange purposes. Was that something you knew of?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally can we just, very quickly, and that is on Vogosca, look at 958D1, 28B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 25th of August, again Mr. Vlaco reporting. Members of the Ilijas SJB arrested three Muslims. Kept in detention for interview. "Twenty men were taken from prison to perform manual work for the Vogosca Brigade." Are you aware of any provision in the law that allows prisoners to be taken off to do manual work for the army?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That runs counter to any convention that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's -- I think this one's already an exhibit. Isn't it? What's 958D1? Well, Your Honours, may I ask the last document be made -- is it not an exhibit? It's certainly a Defence document. It's not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have -- if that is the case, can we have both documents, the previous one 955 and 958, exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours, yes, can we have all three exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And all three are to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then 65 ter 20204 shall be given Exhibit P2367. 955D1 is Exhibit P2368. And 958D1 is P2369. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Coming back to the matter to which we referred at the very beginning about the possible start of the Zupljanin Defence before the Stanisic Defence would have closed, perhaps counsel could, during the break, consult and agree a date when we can formally convene, in advance of the 11th of July, to make any orders, any consequential orders, as are necessary to facilitate that. So we take the 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the break we've discussed the question of timing for discussions and all counsel agreed Monday would be a suitable date, if Your Honours are happy with that, this Monday, when, by which time, Mr. Zecevic ought to have perhaps more information about Mr. Macar. Your Honours, secondly, during the break I was given information that there was a video that we had, which has not been disclosed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Instead of Monday, we think the Tuesday may, perhaps, be more convenient for everyone concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're happy with that. Yes, I see the Defence nodding. Your Honours, I was just about to say that during the break I was given information that there was a video which actually showed the Brano, whichever, the Vlaco - whether it's Branislav, Branko, whatever, Brane - who was the prison warden. I've shown it to Mr. Zecevic and he's happy for me to show it to the witness just to make sure that this is the prison warden we're talking about, however it's fairly obvious it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And is that of any assistance?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't think it is. But Mr. Zecevic says he may as well say this is the Vlaco that was the prison warden. It's got the 65 ter number, now, 20215, and its number was V-- ERN number was V000-5710 and we'll give the Defence a full copy at a later date or at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I'm just going to ask you to look at a short video-clip for the time being, which is 20215, and I just want you to tell us whether you recognise this man.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's Brane Vlaco who was the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you repeat his first name again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brane Vlaco, or Branko Vlaco, which I later heard he was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, which is it, Brane or Branko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branko Vlaco.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You called him Brane, is Brane a short form or could be a nickname, all these Bs, of Branko? Is that how you knew him, Brane?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called him Brane, but his name is Branko. I explained earlier on about this being a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask, for the moment, this be marked for identification only. There's more on this video, and, as I say, this all came up rather suddenly on the break and I want to look at it and it may be we can deal with it with another witness, and equally the Defence may want to deal with it, so could it just be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2370 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I want to move to a different topic, please, and that's the question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, just that we have the P number because it wasn't recorded, for the previous --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could the Registrar please repeat the P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2370.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move to the topic of prosecutions. You were shown by the Defence a document which has got the 65 ter number 385. It's document 25 in our bundle, but it's also in the Defence bundle, I think. It's not 385; it's got a D number now. It was one of ours. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's 1D188.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it's tab 20 in the witness's binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were shown this, Mr. Tusevljak, by Mr. Zecevic, you agreed that this was one of your reports, even though it's undated and unsigned, and established that it must have been sometime after the 25th of August because of something that's said. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And that's why the witness is not responding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Is there a problem with the interpretation, please? The witness says he didn't get any, nor did I, actually. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I hear it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This document, do you remember, you were asked about by Mr. Zecevic, it's between pages 22294 and -7 of the transcript, and you said although this report is not signed nor dated, it's clearly one of your reports submitted to, presumably, Mr. Cvijetic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report from the centre area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we go, please, in English to the second -- sorry, third page, and in B/C/S I think it's the second page. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see, at the top, "Sarajevo CSB. Three reports were submitted for which two were for war crimes against the civilian population." And I'll come back to those reports later. Then no information about crimes recorded in Stari Grad, et cetera. Then on the 25th of August, 1992, that's why I say this report is obviously after that, there's a complaint that the centre received an incorrect memo. And you then go on, or whoever wrote this report: "Taking into consideration the information we have about the non-functioning of the courts and prosecutors' offices on the territories of the municipalities of Bratunac, Skelani, Zvornik, Sekovici, Vlasenica, Ilijas, et cetera, we could have acted in a similar manner." Now, I want you just, please, to have a look at two of the prosecutor's log-books, the KT books for two of the areas you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, could we have up the Zvornik book, which is 65 ter 1555. And it's at tab 55 of our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document on the screen, Your Honours, I note that there is an interpretation, I think, mistake because just as Ms. Korner read the part of the document, it said that they received on the 25th of August from the Ministry of Justice a document or said document which they find incorrect. However, the Serbian word in the original document is "nekorektno," which has a slightly different meaning. Perhaps the interpreters can help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can -- can -- would the best thing would be if the witness reads just that line on the twenty -- from "on the 25th of August, 1992"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just read out what is written until the words "Ministry of Justice."

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 25th of August, 1992, the centre received the letter from the Ministry of Justice number 01-183 dated the 19th of August, 1992, which we assess to be very" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This could either mean unfair or disrespectful, or inaccurate/incorrect, depending on the context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you can stop. That's all we needed. Thank you. Well, I -- perhaps the best thing is to ask you. We don't want details of the memo because it's not relevant, but do you remember what memo this was about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. It would be impossible for me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Don't worry. Right, you've got the Zvornik KT book. And I think it's probably easier for you to look at the print-out that we've got.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we can go, on the screen, please, to 0 -- the number at the top should read 0504-9739. If the usher could ... could we go, on e-court, please, to that page. Can we just highlight the column. Yes, the third column down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that the prosecutor's office in Zvornik was receiving at least a report by the 6th of May on that page ... if we can highlight, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that the public security station filed the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I have that back, please. Now could we have up the Vlasenica KT book, which is P1446, tab 54 of our bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something. Now that I'm looking at this, I would like to interpret something here. The 6th of May, that's when the criminal report was filed by the CSB. If you look at the continuation, the 6th of March, 1998, was the day the prosecutor first started on this report and forwarded the case file to Novi Sad. The next report, again, for the first time the prosecutor acts on the previous report on the 19th of October, 1992, and then on the 28th of June, 1993, was the next time. Next report, the first time the prosecutor follows this up is on the 12th of August, 1992, and next time after that, the 15th of July, 1994. Next report, the date is the 29th of June, again the prosecutor takes it up on this date stated here and then the 6th of May after that. So that's what I'm talking about. This shows you what the prosecutor's office does and how long it takes them to start doing something about a report previously filed by this station. That was the problem. It's not that no one was there in the prosecutor's office. My apologies, I'm just looking at this material.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. I accept entirely that's what it shows. And, I'm sorry, in that case I understand you to be saying there were no prosecutor's office operating, but you're saying just that they didn't do anything when they got the reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about one of my reports, the non-functioning. I'm not sure what the interpretation was that you got. The report that you were showing, our report, shows at page 1 how many criminal reports were filed by each of the police stations. It's clearly reflected there. Filed or submitted to someone, obviously. At the end of the report we clearly state that the reports being filed by us are not being followed through, were not being followed through, and there was a problem obviously. And there were perpetrators there that no measures were being taken against. You saw that case of rape from Bratunac that we discussed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, don't, please, go on. I understand what you're saying very clearly. You're saying you put the reports in, there was a prosecutor's office, but the prosecutor's office did nothing? You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that, although -- I'm not going to bother with the next document now, then, because in the light of this answer, but the Vlasenica KT book has not -- sorry, the Zvornik KT book has not yet received an exhibit number. It's got the 65 ter number 1555. It's all that's been disclosed, and I ask that now, that now that be admitted and exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we had the number of witnesses from Zvornik including the OTP witness who is -- who was a prosecutor in Zvornik, and it wasn't exhibited then. This qualifies as fresh evidence absolutely, in my opinion. And just for -- just because of the principle I object because it's a fresh evidence, otherwise I don't have an objection. And maybe what I suggest is that we MFI it and then I discuss with Ms. Korner and we might stipulate to that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I say that the reason it's come up again is because of this report which the Defence, in fact, produced through this witness and which might have led somebody to believe that it was saying that there was no prosecutor's office operating. A number of the books are exhibited. I think, again, it was a question of trying to keep the documents limited. But I'm perfectly prepared to say at this stage let's just MFI it, and if Mr. Zecevic wants to discuss it then we'll see where we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can you remind me the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is at tab 55 of our documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we adopt counsel's suggestion and we mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2371 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I now want to look with you, leading on from prosecutions to the topic, please, of prosecutions for war crimes and look at this chronologically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up first on the screen, please, P173, which is, sorry, at tab 4 of our binder. Actually, Your Honours, sorry, before we move on to that, although -- the last document, although the Defence showed it to this witness, that's the document that led to all this, the report, it was never actually exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1D188. It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was exhibited before. It was just shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 1D188.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, this document, Mr. Tusevljak, I take it you've seen that one before?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document went to the chiefs of the centres, specifically, I'm not sure I've seen it before, the 16th of May. I still wasn't with the Security Services Centre formally at the time, but I can have a look if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just have a look and see if Mr. Cvijetic at any time discussed with you this order. Just the first paragraph is all that I'm concerned about. And the fourth.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not speak to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So are you saying you were unaware that Mr. Stanisic on the 16th of May had issued an order that documentation should be collected on the crimes against the Serbian population for the purposes of prosecution and to accurately inform the local and international public?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to item number IV on page 3 in English and the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Measures and activities conducted to document war crimes. These activities must involve collection of information and documents on war crimes against Serbs. This implies conducting an on-site investigation," et cetera. Did Mr. Cvijetic, without telling you that this was an order from Mr. Stanisic, ever tell you that one of the tasks was this question of documenting war crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another order, I don't know from which month, which states that we should collect crimes committed against Serbs and all other crimes. And then in July we even distributed the instructions on the procedure. Later on they were accompanied with forms to be filled in. I don't know exactly what was the designation of the forms. But on the 16th of May, the crime prevention police did not really exist within the Security Services Centre. They physically did not exist. So I wouldn't know whether this was forwarded to other police stations, whether we can maybe see it from the stamp denoting the distributions in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. And, yes, we've seen the other orders that you're talking about. As I understand what you're saying about this, in summary, is that you were collecting information from Serbs who were fleeing areas that came under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the TO, in order to launch prosecutions because in those areas there would be no prosecutions for crimes against Serbs. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we, first of all, collected information on crimes committed. However, there were very, very few criminal investigations instigated. The information that we collected was normally forwarded to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think you misunderstand. The -- as I understood what you were saying, the concentration that is displayed by some of the documents on collecting information about war crimes committed against Serbs, you say, is because the areas in which Serbs were being the victims, which were under the control of the Army of BiH or the TO, there would be no prosecutions there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that you personally yourselves in the areas which were under Serb control did not discriminate at all in the criminal charges that you filed or brought; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases we were informed that the crime had been committed, that the corpse was found, belonging to a Bosniak, a Serb, or a Croat, then the forensics would go out on site, on authorisation by the investigative judge, and then there would be an on-site investigation, documents would have been gathered --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Tusevljak. You told us all this. It's a simple question: Your evidence is to the effect that you didn't discriminate, did you? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. Well, let's just have a look at some of the documents, shall we, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at 20169, which is document number 5 in our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a criminal report dated the 14th of June, and handwritten at the top is "received in the public prosecutor's office on the 23rd of June." And this is the Sarajevo one temporarily in Sokolac. It's a criminal report filed against five people; is that right, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you can see from the criminal report itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And it refers to, obviously, would you agree, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that when you look at the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it refers to the offence is slaughtering, brutally killed by torturing and slaughtering, eight Serbian civilians in Gorazde, or from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go, please, in English to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does this show that the allegation or the suggestion, given that the prosecutor decides, from Mr. Cvijetic who signed this -- well, I'll tell you in a minute. The allegation of the crime is a war crime against the civilian population under Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see the second page in my language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's go to the second page in your language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you'll see it's actually signed, type-signed, for Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but his signature is not here, which means that this could probably be the draft version of this document. And I have to say one other thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just stop. No, no, Mr. Tusevljak, let's stick with the draft. At the bottom is written, in handwriting, "a copy was delivered to the Sokolac prosecutor's OJT on the 30th of November as supplementary information to the criminal report"; correct? And if we go back to the first page for you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Go back to the first page in B/C/S, please, and in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here on the second page you can see another piece of handwriting and from that you can see that this copy was re-sent in 1993 because it had been lost somewhere. It was re-sent in November 1993. So this means that the whole case file was re-sent. That's one thing. Another thing, this criminal report, and I know that because of the job that I'm doing, has not been processed to this very day. There are videos from the then television showing the boy who was killed and you can see that he was slaughtered. His throat was slit. And then, listen, you just have to take a look at the ages of the people mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, stop, please. I'm not interested in, for these purposes - as I say, if Mr. Zecevic is, he can re-examine on it - as to what's happened to it since. I'm asking you whether this report -- and if you look at the top, it says "received at the public prosecutor's office on the 23rd of June, 1992," and there's a signature, Milana Mijatovic. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that somebody wrote this, but there is no incoming stamp. There is a stamp in the prosecutor's office of rectangular shape which states received on such and such a date. These things are not handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody merely stated this, but this is not it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. However, as you tell us you're familiar with the case from your present job, it's clear, is it, that this report, whether it had to be re-filed in 1993, was a report sent up by Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be, please, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any objection to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
