utterances.text: And would you further agree that when you were referring in this -- the document that we looked at earlier to three reports submitted, two were for war crimes, one of the reports must have been this one? Mr. Tusevljak, when you referred in that report drafted sometime after the 25th of August to the Sarajevo area, you said that -- sorry, the report said, not you personally, three reports were submitted, two for war crimes. Do you agree this must have been one of them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Next let's go, please, to document which is P275 at tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the record of the minutes of the Presidency on the 17th of June, 1992, item number 3, that the government draft decision on the establishment of a state documentation centre which will gather all genuine documents on crimes committed against the Serbian people during this war. Were you aware of this at the time, Mr. Tusevljak, of this decision? It's either yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, is that the documentation centre which you now work for or run?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, please, can we look at the 11th of July meeting in Belgrade, which you've already commented on. That is P160. We've got it in as number 7, and I can't remember, I'm afraid, what number it was in the Defence binder which you've got. It's document 153 if you want it on -- look at it in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's document 153 in our binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just said that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I was trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's okay. Can we go, please, in English to page 19 and in B/C/S to page 18. Actually, I think it's -- sorry, it's starts at 17 in B/C/S. Yes, that's right. That's the one. No, that's fine, sorry, that was the one I wanted. No. What page is that? It's 1866 -- sorry, no, it should say 1867 on the top. So it's obviously three pages on from the B/C/S version, please. Yeah. No, can we go, sorry, page 19 in English. So it's the page before, in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, the assistant minister for crime affairs, spoke, before we get to you, and at the end he is talking about the document -- obviously I've got a slightly different version here. All right. "Our priority is to document war crimes (on-site investigations, taking photographs, expert analysis, medical reports), and we also need to make lists of war criminals and distribute them to the centres." Then Mr. Kljajic spoke and then you spoke, Mr. Tusevljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go, in English, over the page, please, and also in B/C/S to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Tusevljak, this: "War crimes are documented even if they are committed by Serbs." I want to know why you used the word "even."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't tell me it's not the right word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see. Either in English text I couldn't find the word "even."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's my English. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you read --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "War crimes committed by Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, no, no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- are also documented."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not "even."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. I'm sorry, yes, for some unknown reason I've got a different translation in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was it necessary -- it makes no odds actually to the question I want to ask. Mr. Tusevljak, why was it necessary to say that war crimes committed by Serbs are also documented? Was it because that it was clear what was being talked about was it was war crimes committed against non-Serbs [sic]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear. I can read it all if necessary. I think it would make things much clearer to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't read it all. I want to know why you were saying -- Mr. Planojevic had talked about it just before you and then Mr. Kljajic spoke, saying that documenting of war crimes is a priority. Why did you feel it necessary to say that war crimes committed by Serbs are also documented?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they are being documented, not that they ought to be documented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. What I'm asking you is why -- if it was always understood that it didn't matter who was the victim of a crime or who had committed the crime, blind justice as it were, why did you feel it necessary to say "war crimes committed by Serbs are also documented"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about 1992. This is just a summary of what I said and it had been taken out of context. Whoever wrote this report only briefly summarised my words. Whatever else I said, I cannot remember right now because of the time distance, however, I do know, based on the information I have seen up until now, that public security stations carried out on-site investigations whenever it was possible for them, even when the crimes were committed by Serbs. I am sorry that we do not have now the registers from some other police stations, or daily logbooks, where one could see that. But it is obvious that at that point in time we had some additional documentation about cases where Serbs had been involved in crime, and if notified, the police went or…crime investigation police if it existed, and if it was possible to go to the site of the event, they would do an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can the witness be instructed to speak more slowly because half of his answer was not recorded and he was mentioning at least two times the crimes committed by Serbs and it was not recorded in the transcript and that was precisely what your question was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps he can repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Not at length, please, Your Honours. You know, I definitely want to finish Mr. Tusevljak today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... has a note, because otherwise we could be here forever and ever on this, all the stuff he says is not being registered, and he could ask about it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, God.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's okay, I heard what you had to say and I'm perfectly fine that we ask that the tape be heard and that we have the -- his answer on the -- the revision of the transcript, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm content with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, while we are at it, at page 48, line 23, you are saying -- you are asking: "Mr. Tusevljak, why was it necessary to say that war crimes committed by Serbs are also documented? Was it because that it was" -- that it was ... just my -- "that it was clear that what was being talked about was that it was war crimes committed against non-Serbs?" You meant Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm now just trying to find the pages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please. It's 49 -- [Microphone not activated] -- the word non-Serbs is at 49/1. You said non-Serbs but I think you meant Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry, Your Honours, I didn't. Oh, yes, sorry, you're quite right, I did mean that. Thank you. I really don't think I need to go back over that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me put the straight question to you, Mr. Tusevljak: Didn't you say that? Didn't you say war crimes are -- war crimes committed by Serbs are also documented because it was clear to you that the discussion in the meeting was concentrating on war crimes committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the purpose of my words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can I just take you back, please, to what you said immediately before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which means we have to go back one page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were giving statistics. You said: "In Vlasenica, for example, of the 73 criminal charges, 23 were pressed against Serbs." None of the charges that you were talking about there as against Serbs involved war crimes, did they? Or, indeed, crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact statistics. We should take a look at the statistical data. I think that there were some criminal reports for murders, and murders were considered crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but not murders of non-Serbs, I'm suggesting. Can we just look at, finally, conclusion number 6 of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, which is at page -- and I'm not sure, as I've got a different English version for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Ms. Korner, I wouldn't like to interrupt you, but you made a suggestion. Perhaps the witness should answer to your suggestion. If you are putting your case to the witness, I think he should be given the opportunity to -- unless it is just a comment for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, it's a question and it's -- wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you -- can you recall - I think that's probably the fairest way of doing it - can you recall now what the facts of those charges were which were levied against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall this, but I also cannot claim the opposite. If we are talking about murders, I can't say anything until we take a look at the documents, why were people indicted or processed and who exactly were the victims. If we talk about five murders, we then have to look at the case files of those five murders. I cannot state with any certainty anything now. It was back in 1992 and it's quite a long time ago. So nobody can say, Yeah, we only did this sort of criminal reports or that sort of criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look now, please, at conclusion number 6 of this meeting, which we will find in B/C/S at -- on the page 1 -- 0324-1873, which should be page 23 at the top. Yeah. And in English I haven't the faintest idea because I appeared to have picked up a different version of the translation. It's the one in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that conclusion is: "Preventing and documenting war crimes and using all legally prescribed resources and methods for documenting such enemy activity (on site investigations)," et cetera, "and filing criminal reports not only against identified perpetrators." Now, doesn't that make it clear by the use of the word "such enemy activity," words, that what the police are being asked to document is war crimes committed against Serbs by persons who were considered to be the enemy?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documenting such activity by the enemy, it's only in relation to the enemy. But there were other dispatches and other conclusions too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but this is the major -- first major meeting of the MUP senior officials since the split apparently, the discussion of war crimes comes up, and it's clear as -- I'm trying to think of what the right expression is. But it couldn't be clearer, could it, Mr. Tusevljak, that the discussion was concentrating on war crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can tell by looking at my discussion, I discussed the crimes committed by Serbs. And this is a conclusion that only addresses enemy activity of the kind, but they are not very specific about what the enemy means, who it is. There are reports being submitted against both known and unidentified perpetrators here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you -- I mean, I say you -- the Serbs in Bosnia and the Serb Republic considered the enemy, didn't you, to be what you described as the Green Berets, HOS, the Patriotic League, and the like, who were operating within the Serbian Republic? You considered them the enemy, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And anybody, effectively, who was a Muslim was described as a member of the Green Berets, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's probably an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we take the break, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, can I give -- Your Honours, I'm reminded - I meant to at the last break and then forgot - to give Mr. Tusevljak the full version of the Muslim from -- the Muslim police officer from the airport to read, just so he can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Zecevic has got an unmarked copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness: Mr. Zecevic says he is happy to have the Zvornik -- the Zvornik KT book admitted. We can lift the MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would live the MFI qualification we put on the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P2371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One more thing. On the 16th of June, the Trial Chamber granted in part Stanisic motion filed on the 14th of June, 2011, to amend its Rule 65 ter list of exhibits and remains seized of the motion with regard to 12 documents which were then not translated. The Chamber notes that the documents are now available in English and would like to ask the Prosecution if it has any objection to the addition of these documents to the Stanisic's Rule 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we give you the answer tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Korner, if I may presume to state the obvious, we expect that, of course, you would complete your

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right, Your Honours. I will because I'm not going to be here tomorrow, so I will be completing this cross-examination. It's what I've been agitating about slightly.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, very quickly, you've just read through the statement of the inspector from the airport. Do you agree now that it does appear that the JNA moved into the airport on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I read the statement and it says that General [as interpreted] Delic's police also stayed at the airport in the police station there until the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's recorded "General Delic." I believe the witness said "Kenan Delic," the statement of Kenan Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I wasn't looking. Yes, Kenan Delic. Yes. Thank you. Can we look now, please, at document which is 65 ter 20156. It's tab 13.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: This, again, is a criminal report against 18 named people. Do we agree that numbers 1 through to 11 of the named people are Muslim and 12 through to 18, Croat? Or 12 through to 17, I think.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if one can see this on the screen, but all these investigations are still in progress. And the BH prosecutor does not show these things because this is confidential. This is still confidential in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's not a good idea to be showing this, I think, because the investigations are still in progress. I do apologise for placing that remark on the record, but that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask that it doesn't -- I suppose it's a bit late, but when the video is shown this doesn't go out on the screen. And I haven't named the people.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Can you just answer my question, Mr. Tusevljak: Are numbers 1 through to 10 -- 11 Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I believe also for the previous criminal complaint that we saw, it's P2372, I don't know, maybe it's too late now, but perhaps we can have that also.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It probably is too late to redact it.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: But thank you, Mr. Tusevljak, for the reminder. Anyway, please, very quickly because I haven't got much time left. 1 to 11 --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And numbers 12 through to 17/18, are they Croat?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but it's difficult to tell because sometimes Serb names and Croat names are not too far apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Ms. Korner, but having regard to what the witness has indicated about the confidentiality of this material, is a redaction of the question and answer necessary? Or is it sufficient for us to have the -- I've been in consultations, as you would have observed, with the Court Officer, and we just wonder you think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I -- did I identify -- I just said it was a criminal report. I don't think I -- and I've just gone back to what I said. So I don't think that that requires to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And apparently no further order of the Chamber is necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can we go, please, to the second page in English and the third page in B/C/S. Sorry, fourth page in B/C/S. No, I'm sorry, stay where we are. Third page in B/C/S and the fourth page in English. Wrong way around.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: It's type-signed Mr. Cvijetic but, in fact, signed on his behalf, and is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And the crime there alleged --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go back to -- no, all right. We're in -- okay. Yeah, in B/C/S, I think, we need to go back to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Was a war crime against the civilian population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I won't go into the details because we're not in private session, but I would ask that this be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2373, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next --

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And just so that we know, this was in July, this report, so would that have been the second report that's referred to in your crime statistics, as it were, that we looked at earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably so.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move now, please, to document 20171, which is at tab 19 of our bundle. Your Honours, this is the document that I looked at very briefly with Mr. Tusevljak yesterday. It's a response. And we'll see there's another document linked with this later. I'm told by Mr. Zecevic that it wasn't disclosed. But, as he puts it, he's feeling kindly disposed to me today and so he's not going to object to taking off the MFI. It was MFI'd as P2362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we lift the MFI qualification on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours will see why, because there is, as I say, a later-linked document. Now, could we look, please, at document which is 1D188, which is at tab 25 and was referred to -- no, I've already had that one. Sorry, forget that. That's the one I've already looked at. Sorry. Can we look, please, at 2031, tab 30. No, sorry, I've made a mistake in my note, I'm told. Oh, I've left out -- it's 20 -- yes, I've transposed something. Sorry, that's not what I want at all. It's 20173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's tab 30?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's tab 30.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, is this a telegram -- is it signed by you or simply going out under your name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went out under my name. It's not my handwriting and it's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: All right. But the date is the 12th of September. It's sent from the Security Services Centre. It says "Everyone"; does that mean it went to all SJBs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be to all public security stations under the Security Services Centre, but it's not my signature. It's not mine. I didn't write it. It was one of my people.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: So are you saying you are unaware of this telegram that went out under your name, saying, "we urge you to send us as soon as possible the attachments to the report on war crimes and genocide against the Serb people on your territory ..."?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the RZ and RZ1 questionnaires. It's probably an urgent matter. So there had to be a broader, more comprehensive dispatch preceding this one.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Okay, well, there may have been, but are you aware of -- were you -- all right, let's put it this way: Were you sending a request to the SJBs within the AOR of the Sarajevo CSB asking for the questionnaires to be filled in?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, again, then, may I ask that it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then have a look, please, at -- sorry, I think it's 142D1, which is at tab 32.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: The telegram that's just been admitted, we probably didn't notice it, said number 01-477/92, and this appears to be the response of Zvornik to your telegram or the dispatch -- I think -- I see what you mean, Mr. Tusevljak, you obviously sent an original dispatch with that number and the telegram was sent as a reminder, because we see "with reference to your dispatch of the 12th of September"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is probably the case.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And then Zvornik says: "On the 26th of June, 1992, we sent the information on genocide committed against the Serbian population on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik to the Bijeljina services centre ..." And this goes back to what we already looked at that you discussed, that they were sending stuff to Bijeljina. "Considering that you most probably did not receive it, we are sending you the photocopy of this information. A criminal report" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: "Criminal reports were not submitted against unknown persons, in other words, Muslim extremists who had committed crimes against the people listed in the information, because" - interestingly enough - "crimes against these people were committed during combat activities and because the military police took their corpses." Right. I think this is already an exhibit. Mr. Tusevljak, you agree, that's the -- do you remember receiving this response from Zvornik to your original dispatch?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I probably received it. This is the Security Services Centre. But the problem with these dispatches, as I pointed out, I can't see the stamp, the one that I've been talking about, the incoming stamp of the Security Services Centre in the upper right-hand corner, but I probably received this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt the witness's answer. The document is Exhibit 1D594. And Ms. Korner in her question was quoting the document as saying "interestingly enough."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, I'm sorry, I meant to say -- I'm not now quoting. That was my own comment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Zecevic is quite right. I interposed that and I shouldn't have, and it was my comment. The document does not say "interestingly enough." Now can we look, please, next at another response to this, your questions, please, it is P1072. Tab 33. P10 -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: This is, again, the response to your original dispatch. This time addressed to you personally. So did you -- do you recall getting this response from Mr. Djuric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. It's all written in the framework of the 01-477 dispatch.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, please, can we look at P793, which is at tab 34.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: This is a copy of the report that went up from the CSB centre for the work between July and September of 1992. We can see at the top it's handwritten Mr. Cvijetic. And I just want to ask you about one part of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on page 6 in English and page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Five, sorry, in B/C/S. Sorry, 5.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And it's the penultimate paragraph. "The documentary material on the genocide against the Serbian people is a separate matter and the sector is putting the maximum effort to ensure this work is carried out and recorded properly." That part of the report would have come from your section, wouldn't it, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. We didn't write this. This is someone from the analytics department of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: But the information about that part would have come from your section; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, based on the dispatches that we sent, 01-477 and things like that, so what is indicated here is probably based on that.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Well, I think, because it's October 1992, we'll see that it comes from you because from looking at the next document, please, which is 20175 and it's at tab 35, it's dated the 6th of October. It's the activity report of the CSB crime department for the period July to September 1992. In fact, I think it was a document that you were asked about when you testified in the Dragomir Milosevic case, weren't you? Do you remember that? This is at page 8052, reference to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically, but the report is in front of me and I challenged nothing about it. This is about the crime prevention measures over these two months.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Exactly. But in paragraph 2 there's a reference to 18 murders and I think you told the Court then that those were nothing to do with war crimes, they were ordinary murders, if I can use that expression? Is that right; those are not -- they're nothing to do with any kind of, as it were, inter-ethnic conflict?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's been a long time. 18 murders, one attempted murder. I can only know what these murders were about if I look at the specific entries. I don't remember. It has been a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: I understand that, but when you testified in the Milosevic case, which was some four years ago now, or thereabouts, let me just put to you what you said. Mr. Tapuskovic asked you, and this is at page 8052: "... you mentioned 18 murders ... can you tell us what kind of murders ... could you explain this to the Judges, please? "A. These were just run-of-the-mill murders," the expression, that's how it was translated, "that had no ethnic base. The ethnicity of the perpetrator or the victim were not a factor, so this was perhaps caused by some property disputes between the victim and the perpetrator or some other cause of this nature. "Q. If we were to look at it in context of the victims in the light of their ethnicity, was it possible to draw the distinction -- to distinguish various victims on the basis of their ethnicity? "A. Well, in most cases the victims were Serbs. As far as I can recall, there were two murders with the Croats and Muslims as victims ... I think ... the perpetrators were apprehended, prosecuted, and sentenced ... "Q. And who were the perpetrators in general terms? "A. Well, for the most part, Serbs were the perpetrators. "Judge Harhoff: Mr. Witness, are we to conclude that the crimes described in your report were unrelated to the war? "A. The 18 murders, yes, that's true." So that's what you said then. Presumably the facts were fresher in your memory. So do you agree that's probably correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so. I did say these things but even then I wasn't able to be really specific. I think this was about the murders at Ilidza and Vogosca and elsewhere where ethnic Bosniaks were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Well, all right: Can we just come to what I really want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's at, in the English, paragraph 3 up from the bottom. Where, as I say, this is obviously the basis of what went into the report. In the B/C/S you'll find it on the second page. B/C/S page 2. Thank you. The paragraph is the third one down on that page.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: "Documenting crimes of genocide and war crimes against the Serbian people constitutes a separate issue and the sector has undertaken maximum effort, in spite of great difficulties, to document these crimes in the proper fashion. In view of that, seven criminal reports have already been submitted to competent prosecutor's offices against 33 persons for whom there are grounds to suspect that they have committed crimes of genocide and war crimes against the Serbian population."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document now be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was this a question or was it a ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I can ask the question, but he's already said this is his report.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Is that what you put into this report, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously. The report is ours, the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2375, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we now have up on the screen, but not to be broadcast, please, because it's a criminal report, and it's document with the number 20178, tab 40.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: This is a document, a report, dated, I think, the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to page 3 in English, please, and both -- and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: This report has gone out under your signature; is that right, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a draft. I don't think I signed it because it was probably renamed into head of the Security Services Centre, Zoran Cvijetic and then he signed it. He also had the authority to file reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to the front page again in both -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Are the alleged perpetrators here Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one that I can see.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: So is that the first one that's named?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, both, both are.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And is the suggested classification of the crime - and I say that because I understand the prosecutor can change this - that these two committed a crime against humanity in the Gorazde municipality? Sorry, the Pale -- sorry, in Pale, not Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would need to see the classification, but I think we are looking at Article 141.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of -- maybe, does it not come out in it B/C/S terribly well? If you look at the very bottom, I think it comes out there, of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, B/C/S. The English is fine. Can we just move the B/C/S up.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: If you look at the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 141 and -42 of the adopted KZ.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Is that still an on-going case?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, still on-going and not resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 66/13, I believe the witness said which KZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Adopted, it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he says adopted KZ of ... so I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, adopted -- repeat, sorry, can you repeat what you said. You read out what is at the bottom. Can you just read that out again.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Article 141 and 142 of the adopted KZ of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, please, could we look at 1D189 -- oh, sorry, Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2376, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, please, could we look at document 1D189. Again not to be shown on the screen because this is the one you raised originally. And, Your Honours, maybe we ought to go into private session just for this document because I want to ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is at tab pre - p-r-e - 1B. Could we go, please, in that report in English to the -- it's page 12 in the -- no. Yes, it's page 12. And in B/C/S to page 13.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, in your copy, if you go to page 13 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. That's page 9 in B/C/S. Page 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: This is the part of the report that deals with your section, is that right, the crime prevention and detection?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at the level of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then go, in English, to three pages further on. It should be page 15 at the bottom, and in B/C/S to page 17 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: And the paragraph that says: "In this period criminal inspectors visited all CSBs, SJBs, had meetings where they gave instructions for carrying out concrete operative activities. The focus of the operative work in the CSBs and SJBs was on detection, documenting, and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, torched or destroyed immovable property, cultural, or religious monuments, and other assets." Do you agree that that's an accurate summary of the focus of the operative work of your section in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, because besides the things are that are mentioned here, they also carried out in other task. So they were not involved only in processing war crimes. The important thing here is to look at all the KU registers. Everything that I looked through told me that if we had 22 police stations and there were four reports in one year, ten reports in another year, and then again four reports - I'm talking about criminal reports for war crimes - and if the total number is around 400 criminal reports for general crime per year, then we are talking about very small percentages. On the other hand, this is a MUP report that I had a chance to read only now because I did not receive it in 1992 and I could not read it in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the sake of the clarity of the transcript, 76/18, I believe the P is 625. It wasn't recorded, the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Now, you had a look through the Sarajevo CSB book, which I gave to you, which only begins, for some reason, in November of 1992, but carries on through till, I think it's 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Was there any record of any criminal reports against Serbs for war crimes, however classified, against non-Serbs in that register?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A murder. Multiple murder.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that is, please? Which number? Did you make a note?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can find it quite easily.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: All right. I'll give you the book back again.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is -- that there are some cases that are still on-going before the courts and prosecutor's offices. If you want, I can quote you those names.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: I just want to know if you can tell me that there's a criminal report --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the witness was suggesting that we go into private session because he wants to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: You can just -- no, we needn't go into private session. You just tell me the number of the -- the thing and then we needn't mention any names. You just tell me the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you -- will you call the exhibit on the screen? Because you gave the copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Sorry. If I can find my list of exhibits. It's Exhibit 20188 at tab 56.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminal report number 5 from 1994 for multiple murders of citizens of Bosniak ethnicity. There is also a judgement. The person in question has already served his sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: All right. Number 5 in 1994; is that right? And can you just -- just tell us: What's the date, please, of the alleged criminal offence? Is it 1992 or is it later?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later. It was later. I can't see the date from this copy when exactly it was committed.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: But it wasn't in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime shortly after 1992. But since this register begins in 1992, there are only three or four reports, and that's the gist of the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: All right. Are there any -- if I didn't make it clear, are there any that you saw, even filed later, that relate to crimes committed in 1992 where the perpetrator alleged is a Serb and the victims are non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are some murders. Criminal reports related to murders. Remember, 36 paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Yes, but we can see that you were charging -- we've just been through a whole set of criminal reports where the allegation that you sent up, whatever the prosecutor did in the end was out of war crimes. Are there any for war crimes? Leave aside the murders under section 36.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've just seen the criminal (redacted).

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, and I cannot speculate whether there were such cases in some other areas. I'm sure that if we examine their KU registers that we would certainly find some cases.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it probably ought to be now properly exhibited, if there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness said that just the first three, four are from 1992. I mean, I don't have a problem that it's exhibited, but it's a lengthy document and without -- without the precise explanation on each and every entry, it doesn't serve us much that we have the 100 pages of a document. Perhaps first two pages and that should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the point I'm making is proving a negative, if you like. Can I leave it this way: Can we mark it for identification at the moment, and I'll discuss it with Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of what would eventually comprise the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So it's so marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed we may be able to do it by an agreed statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2382 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention in the transcript: Page 80 at 1 it should be recorded as an answer to the witness. The question was: "Are there any for war crimes? Leave aside the murders under section 36." And then: "We've just seen (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was the answer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And it probably ought to be redacted because if you will recall Mr. Tusevljak wanted to deal with that in private session. So can we redact that. Just that last. Once it's properly recorded as an answer, it ought to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE TIME WE RISE
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, let's final this, because I ought to make it clear to you: I'm suggesting that it's quite clear -- and I'm not -- I'm not suggesting this is what you wanted to happen, but it's quite clear that your clear instructions from your bosses from, I suggest, the minister downwards was to investigate war crimes against Serbs and effectively not to bother with the war crimes that were committed against the non-Serbs? And that's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Investigations were conducted in other cases of crimes, not only when it's about Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. -- that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment to tomorrow -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we perhaps ask Mr. Zecevic how long re-direct will take? Just for planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honours, one session, perhaps less than that or perhaps a bit more. But before that, I don't think that the answer was recorded properly, 81/20. I believe the witness said when the victims were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, he did. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Your Honours, may I apologise for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- not being able to be here tomorrow. I have, unfortunately, something I can't get out of, and I didn't want to ask Your Honours to sit late. And Ms. Pidwell, who's been following this, will take over for re-examination if Your Honours will agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent that you need the Court's leave, you have it, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think -- but politely I ought to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And we are grateful for the interpreters, the court reporter, and the security and support staff for the additional few minutes that we would have sat this afternoon. So we take the adjournment to reconvene tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
